dialogue_tree.speaker: General O'Neill
dialogue_tree.text: So. You're the one from the ship. The one billions of light years away. Welcome to Earth. Try not to break anything.

dialogue_tree.speaker: General O'Neill
dialogue_tree.text: CO2 scrubbers failed. Classic. You know, we had a similar problem on Prometheus. Half the crew passed out before someone thought to crack a window. You found lime on a planet? That's resourceful. That's the kind of thinking that keeps people alive out there.

dialogue_tree.speaker: General O'Neill
dialogue_tree.text: Hull integrity at what percentage? And you're telling me the ship is billions of years old and still flying? Either the Ancients built things to last, or you're the luckiest crew in the galaxy. Probably both. Keep the power grid stable. We can't send you parts from here.

dialogue_tree.speaker: General O'Neill
dialogue_tree.text: Aliens. Of course there are aliens. It wouldn't be a proper deep-space mission without something trying to kill you. Document everything. If you encounter a race that can help, negotiate. If they shoot first... well, you know what to do.

dialogue_tree.speaker: General O'Neill
dialogue_tree.text: Supplies. Right. I'll see what I can do, but understand — the stones are your only link. We can't exactly FedEx you a care package through a wormhole. What I can send is intelligence. SGC databases, star charts, anything the Ancients left behind that we've decoded. I'll have Dr Brightman set it up.

ambient_lines: Why is the coffee always cold?
Every time someone says 'Ancient technology,' something explodes.

dialogue_tree.speaker: Dr Brightman
dialogue_tree.text: Ah. The communication stones. You must be from the Destiny expedition. Take your time adjusting — the disorientation passes. I've been through it myself. Tell me, what have you found out there?

dialogue_tree.speaker: Dr Brightman
dialogue_tree.text: A CO2 scrubber failure on a ship that old? The Ancient life-support systems must have degraded past their backup capacity. Lime as a chemical scrubber substitute — that's brilliant, actually. The calcium oxide reaction is exothermic but effective. I'll cross-reference our database for any Ancient filtration schematics that might help you repair the original system.

choices.text: What else can you tell me?

dialogue_tree.speaker: Dr Brightman
dialogue_tree.text: The ship's power systems are running on residual energy from a star? That's consistent with what we theorized about Ancient vessel design. The Destiny-class ships were meant to run autonomously for millions of years. If you can restore even partial power to the main reactors, you'll extend your operational window significantly.

choices.text: What else can you tell me?

dialogue_tree.speaker: Dr Brightman
dialogue_tree.text: Fascinating. Non-humanoid life, you say? And the planet had ruins? The Destiny's mission was to seed Stargates and explore — it was always possible you'd encounter evidence of prior civilizations. I'll flag your report for the xenobiology team. Any biological samples you can bring back through the gate would be invaluable.

choices.text: What else can you tell me?

dialogue_tree.speaker: Dr Brightman
dialogue_tree.text: I'll compile a data package — Ancient language databases, star charts from the SGC archives, and any technical manuals we've decoded. The General authorized it. I'll transmit through the next stone link. Be careful out there. The data is valuable, but your crew is more so.

ambient_lines: The stones are remarkably stable today.
I should check the calibration readings.
Dr Jackson would want to hear about this.

dialogue_tree.speaker: Maryann
dialogue_tree.text: Oh! You startled me. Your eyes — you're not... you're from out there, aren't you? Eli's out there. On that ship. Is he okay? Please, tell me he's okay.

choices.text: I can't promise anything, but he's fighting.

dialogue_tree.speaker: Maryann
dialogue_tree.text: Alive. Thank God. When they told me about Icarus — the base, the attack — I thought... I thought I'd never see him again. He's just a boy. He plays video games. He shouldn't be on a spaceship billions of light years from home.

choices.text: He's saved all of us more than once.
I'll tell him you're proud of him.

dialogue_tree.speaker: Maryann
dialogue_tree.text: He saved you? That sounds like Eli. Always solving puzzles, always figuring things out. Even when he was little, he'd take apart the VCR and put it back together. I just... I wish I could tell him I'm proud of him. The real him. Not just the version the Air Force lets me see on the news.

choices.text: I'll tell him you're proud of him.

dialogue_tree.speaker: Maryann
dialogue_tree.text: Stronger than I think. You're right. He always was. I just worry. That's what mothers do. But knowing he's out there, fighting, solving problems... that's my boy. That's my Eli.

choices.text: I'll tell him you're proud of him.

dialogue_tree.speaker: Maryann
dialogue_tree.text: You'll tell him? Please do. Tell him his mom loves him. Tell him... tell him I know he can do this. And tell him to call me if he ever figures out how. I'll be right here. Waiting.

dialogue_tree.speaker: Maryann
dialogue_tree.text: Thank you. For coming. For telling me. I know this — the stones, the body swap — it must be strange. But for a mother who thought her son was dead... this means everything. Take care of him out there. Please.

ambient_lines: Eli, if you can hear me...
I baked cookies. He always loved cookies.
The news never says what's really happening.

sgc_briefing_lines: The briefing room is quiet. A long table. Maps of the galaxy on the walls. Coffee stains on the wood.
Through the window, you can see the Stargate — silent, standing in its chamber below.
General O'Neill sits at the head of the table, fingers laced, watching you with tired eyes.
Dr Brightman stands by a console, data scrolling past. She nods when she sees you looking.
personal_moment_lines: The apartment is small. Warm. Photos on the refrigerator — Eli, younger, grinning at the camera.
A gaming headset sits on the couch. A half-finished crossword puzzle on the coffee table.
The smell of something baking. Home. A place that exists only in memory, now made real through the stones.
